title: Shadowbench: kernel cascade under mixed-precision bursts (INT8/GPTQ/AWQ)
content:
Summary:
This is a working note for the "shadowbench" experiment: a targeted benchmark to reproduce and characterize latency/quality regressions that appear when kernel selection flips under mixed-precision profiles (INT8 / GPTQ / AWQ / FP8). The goal is to capture failure modes caused by small background bursts (tiny priming requests, attention-sparsity outliers) that trigger a cascade of kernel switches and KV-cache thrash, resulting in P95/P99 latency spikes and occasional quality regressions.

Motivation / why this doc exists:
- We keep seeing intermittent customer incidents where overall throughput is fine but tail latency spikes unexpectedly for multiworkload hosts.
- Hypothesis: memory layout changes and kernel switchover (fast path -> fallback path) create transient pathologies amplified by quantized kernels (especially AWQ/GPTQ combos).
- Need a repeatable microbenchmark + failure catalogue to inform mitigations (routing stickiness, cache prewarm, kernel hysteresis).

Hypotheses to test:
1) Small warmup requests that change attention sparsity cause per-layer kernel selection to oscillate, forcing slower kernels and KV invalidations.
2) Mixed-precision routing (e.g., when some shards use AWQ and others GPTQ) increases cache footprint and IO pressure, causing kernel scheduling jitter on NPU/GPU lanes.
3) FP8 fallback (when detected numeric instability) causes synchronous slow path execution on a subset of layers, magnifying tail latency.

Testbed / hardware:
- Instance: dedicated GPU nodes (A100-40GB + 2x CPU cores pinned to serving process) and smaller T4 test group for edge cases.
- Runtime: serving-runtime branch shadowbench/experiment-04 (see PR 578).
- Driver stack: CUDA 11.8, cuBLAS 11.10, custom kernel library v0.9.2-shadow.
- Model: open-weights Llama-family 13B distilled checkpoint (consistent with production 13B-ish workloads), plus a 70B probe in isolated runs to check scale effects.

Workload design (shadowbench pattern):
- Steady-state: high-frequency short prompts (avg length 30 tokens) from workload A (embedding-ish chat).
- Shadow bursts: interleaved low-rate long-context (1000 tokens) prompts every 2-5s to simulate heavy KV use.
- Noise injections: occasional synthetic attention sparsity token sequences designed to push certain attention kernels into fallback.
- Multiplexing: mixing requests that prefer AWQ-quantized model shards with requests pinned to GPTQ shards.

Configuration matrix (high level):
- Quant modes: INT8 (symmetric), GPTQ (per-channel), AWQ (4-bit-like), FP8 (fallback simulation).
- Kernel sets: fast-vectorized, tiled-fallback, fallback-with-accumulator-locks.
- Batching: single-request (no batch), micro-batch (2-8), continuous-batch-enabled (client-side concatenation).
- Cache: prefix-kv enabled vs disabled, small-KV eviction aggressive vs conservative.

Metrics we capture:
- Latency: p50, p90, p95, p99 per-request and per-token.
- Throughput: tokens/sec aggregated and by-request-type.
- Kernel switch events: timestamped logs whenever layer kernel selection changes from fast->fallback or vice versa.
- KV cache hit/miss, eviction counts.
- Output quality: simple metric = normalized cross-entropy against reference for seeded prompts + BLEU-like match on deterministic tasks.

Key observations (first pass):
- When shadow bursts are enabled, p95 increases by 1.8-3x depending on quant mode. AWQ+GPTQ mixed runs showed the worst tail behavior.
- Kernel switch logs correlate tightly with p95 spikes: a cluster of fast->fallback flips within 100ms precede a spike.
- KV eviction rate increases when mixed quant shards are present — suggests higher memory fragmentation.
- FP8 fallback simulated path toggles a global mutex in the runtime that serializes some layer execution; this appears to be the single largest contributor to a sustained tail.

Representative numbers (13B runs, averaged over 10 trials):
- Baseline (INT8 uniform, no shadow bursts): p95 = 210ms, throughput = 160 tok/s
- Shadow enabled + AWQ/GPTQ mix: p95 = 560ms, throughput = 120 tok/s, KV evictions +220%
- FP8-fallback forced: p95 transient peaked at 1.2s for ~300ms windows, kernel switch count +7x

Root-cause hypotheses refinement:
- Primary driver: kernel-selection oscillation due to local per-layer heuristics that don't account for cross-request interference. When one request forces a fallback, heuristics on subsequent requests flip back and forth as micro-batches interleave.
- Secondary driver: increased working set from mixed quantization leads to elevated GPU memory churn and allocator fragmentation, increasing eviction and kernel overhead.
- Tertiary: serialization path introduced by FP8 numeric stabilization path (mutex / single-thread fallback) causes global blocking for a subset of layers.

Mitigation ideas (ranked):
1) Kernel hysteresis: require stable metric for N successive decisions before switching kernel at layer granularity (soft-sticky kernels). Low-cost and effective in early tests (reduced flip rate by ~65%).
2) Per-request kernel pinning for the duration of a session when request pattern shows temporal locality (e.g., same client conversation).
3) Allocator improvements: prefer compact allocation for mixed-quant loads, trigger compaction during low-load windows.
4) Defer FP8 stabilization to background warming; do not flip to FP8 path synchronously mid-request (convert to async prewarm).
5) Route heavy long-context requests to specialized dedicated pools to avoid contaminating multi-tenant GPU working sets.

Short experiment notes / quick wins tested:
- Hysteresis implementation (branch 578) reduced observed flip clusters and cut p95 by ~30% on AWQ/GPTQ mix in preliminary runs.
- Pinning kernels per-session improved tail when session stickiness existed but increased average latency slightly for single-shot workloads.

Open questions and unknowns:
- How well do these mitigations scale to 70B class models? We ran a few isolated probes but need dedicated capacity tests.
- Are there kernel microarchitectural interactions (SM scheduling) that cause non-linear amplification at high concurrency? (needs low-level profiler traces)
- Long-term cost impact: does routing heavy requests to dedicated pools materially increase unit cost for typical customers?

Action items / next steps:
- (Priya) Add continuous kernel-switch telemetry per-layer to the main ingestion pipeline (ENG-1298). Due: 2024-04-25.
- (Tom) Run controlled 70B runs on staging with hysteresis enabled to validate scaling. Due: 2024-05-02.
- (Miguel) Prototype allocator compaction experiment and measure fragmentation metrics. Due: 2024-04-30.
- (Aisha) Draft short user-facing note about routing long-context heavy requests to dedicated pools and how that affects tail latency. Due: 2024-04-28.

Notes / informal observations:
- This doc is intentionally rough — lots of TODOs and half-formed experiments.
- Slack convo: see #serving-runtime thread from 2024-04-10 for raw flame graphs and sample logs.
